# Brighten image

- Route: `/tools/brighten-image`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `brighten-image`

## Summary

Lift a dark photo with a real exposure control in linear light, or with Brightness and Shadows when you want a gentler, more selective change. (Photo editing)

## Details

A dark photo can be brightened in three different ways, and they do not look the same. The Exposure (EV) slider in the Basic panel of Aperture works in linear light, the way a camera stop does: +1 EV doubles the light at every pixel, so shadows and midtones rise proportionally while already bright areas clip to white sooner. The Brightness slider adds a fixed amount to the sRGB value instead, which lifts blacks the most and looks flatter. The Shadows slider in the Tone group raises only the dark end, weighted by luminance, and leaves the highlights where they were. This page explains the math of each, with the numbers, so you can choose the one that matches the photo in front of you.
### What it does
- Exposure (EV) from -5 to +5: decodes each channel from sRGB to linear light, multiplies by 2 to the power EV, adds the Offset, re-encodes, then applies Gamma. One stop is a doubling, exactly as on a camera.
- Brightness from -100 to +100 in the Light group: adds the value divided by 200 to the sRGB channel before the contrast step, so +50 adds 0.25, which is about 64 levels on an 8-bit scale, to every pixel that has room.
- Shadows from -100 to +100 in the Tone group: a luminance-weighted lift that is strongest at black, fades to nothing at a luma of 0.6, and scales all three channels together so colors keep their hue.
- Each control is its own adjustment layer, so a +1 EV layer and a Shadows +40 layer can be masked, blended and switched off independently.
- The histogram under the panels updates as you drag, so you can see when the right edge starts to pile up against white and back off before anything clips.
### How to use it
1. Open the dark photo: Drop a JPG, PNG, WebP or AVIF, or sign in for HEIC and TIFF. The Basic panel is in front.
2. Set the exposure: Drag Exposure (EV) toward +1 while watching the histogram. Stop when the midtones sit where you want them, even if the darkest corners are still murky.
3. Open the shadows: Use Shadows in the Tone group for the remaining dark areas. It only touches pixels below a luma of 0.6, so the sky and skin highlights stay put.
4. Check and export: Hold the backslash key to compare with the original, then export. The server re-renders the original at full size with the same two formulas.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- Exposure and Tone are per-pixel operations with no neighborhood, so the preview is instant at any size and the export time is dominated by decoding and encoding the file.
- Brightening an 8-bit source cannot create detail that was clipped to black in the camera; a region recorded as 0, 0, 0 stays neutral and only rises with Offset or Brightness.
### Technical details
- Exposure per channel: linear = sRGB decode of v, then clamp(linear times 2 to the power EV plus Offset) to 0 to 1, encode back to sRGB, then raise to the power 1 / Gamma. The decode uses v / 12.92 below 0.04045 and ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) to the power 2.4 above it.
- Because the multiply happens in linear light, a mid gray of 0.5 (128 of 255) becomes 0.686 (175) at +1 EV, 0.801 (204) at +1.5 EV and 0.934 (238) at +2 EV, while 0.8 (204) is already clipped to 1.0 at +1 EV.
- Brightness and Contrast share one layer: v = clamp(v + brightness / 200), then (v - 0.5) times 2 to the power (contrast / 50) plus 0.5. With Contrast at 0 the second step is the identity, so Brightness +25 adds exactly 0.125 to every channel that has room.
- Shadows: with L the BT.709 luma, the weight is 1 - smoothstep(0, 0.6, L) and the luma change is 0.25 times shadows / 100 times that weight. The new luma divided by the old luma (floored at 0.0001) scales all three channels, so a pixel with luma 0.1 gets a weight of 0.926 and rises to 0.216 at Shadows +50.
- The preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy; the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance of a few 8-bit levels at most (grain is exact). An exposure change on its own typically matches to the level.
- Offset (-0.5 to +0.5) adds in linear light after the multiply, which is why a small value such as 0.05 turns pure black 0 into 0.248 (63): it is a floor lift, not a brightening, and is mainly useful for matte looks.
### When not to use it
If the photo is bright enough but looks dull, you do not need to brighten it at all; the contrast page or a curve is the right fix, and adding exposure will only push the highlights into white. A photo whose shadows are solid black with no texture cannot be rescued by any slider, because an 8-bit JPEG stores nothing below zero. And for a photo that is dark only in the corners, the Vignette slider at a positive amount is a cleaner, edge-weighted brightening than a global exposure change.
### Use cases
- Indoor photo that came out dark: Exposure +1.2 EV with Shadows +40 recovers a dim living room shot; the lamp highlights will clip, so add a radial mask around the lamp with the Exposure layer subtracted inside it.
- Backlit portrait: Leave Exposure at 0 so the window stays white rather than blown out, and add a Shadows +60 Tone layer for the face, or paint a brush mask over the face on an Exposure +1 layer.
- Scanned print that reads gray: A scan that is dark overall but has no true blacks responds better to Brightness -10 with Contrast +20 than to exposure, because the problem is a lifted floor, not a lack of light.
- Screenshot or flat graphic: For artwork with flat fills, Brightness +15 adds the same 0.075 to every color and keeps the fills uniform, where an exposure change would alter them unevenly.
### FAQ
Q: What does +1 EV do to a pixel?
A: It doubles the pixel in linear light. On the sRGB scale that is not a doubling: 0.5 becomes 0.686, 0.2 becomes 0.285, and 0.8 is clipped to 1.0. Values are clamped to 0 to 1 after the multiply, so anything that would exceed white is lost unless you lower the exposure or mask the area.
Q: Why does Brightness look flatter than Exposure?
A: Brightness adds the same amount to every channel in sRGB: +25 adds 0.125 to a black of 0 and to a gray of 0.5 alike, so the floor rises and the picture loses contrast. Exposure multiplies in linear light, which keeps dark tones dark relative to light ones.
Q: How far can I brighten before it falls apart?
A: Up to about +1.5 EV an 8-bit JPEG usually holds, though shadow noise becomes visible. Beyond +2 EV, banding appears in smooth gradients because the file only had 256 levels to begin with. The Noise reduction and Grain layers in the Detail panel can hide some of this.
Q: Can I brighten only part of the photo?
A: Yes. Add the Exposure layer, then give it a mask: a linear gradient for a dark foreground, a brush for a face, a luminosity range for everything below a chosen brightness, or Select subject for the main object. The adjustment only applies where the mask is white.
Q: Does brightening change the colors?
A: Exposure and Shadows scale red, green and blue together, so hue is preserved until a channel clips. Brightness also adds equally to the three channels, which slightly desaturates strong colors as they approach white. If you see a color shift, lower the amount or switch the layer blend to Luminosity.
Q: Is the exported photo brighter by exactly the same amount as the preview?
A: Yes, within one or two 8-bit levels. The server runs the identical exposure decode, multiply and encode on the full-resolution original, in float64 for photos up to 4 megapixels, and the deploy selftest verifies it against stored golden renders.
